title: Assessing Bird and Bat Mortality at the McEvoy Ranch Wind Turbine in Marin County, California

## Introduction

In the midst of increasing public awareness of problems associated with climate change, alternative energy sources have received strong public interest.  While wind energy may provide environmental benefits and has generally been considered a favorable alternative to fossil fuels, the negative impacts of wind energy development on birds and bats due to mortality at turbines have raised important ecological considerations. On local scales, studies of wind turbine effects on bird and bat mortality range from reporting very little or no impact (Anderson et al. 1996, Strickland et al. 1996) to relatively high impact (Orloff and Flannery 1992).  On larger scales, estimates of fatal bird collisions with wind turbines across the U.S. range from 10,000 (Erickson et al. 2001) to 573,000 birds annually (Smallwood 2013), and Loss et al. (2013) estimates bird deaths in the U.S. caused by monopole turbines alone is between 140,000 and 328,000 birds annually.  In order to address concerns regarding potential conflicts between wind turbines and wildlife, preliminary site assessments should be conducted at proposed wind turbine sites to assess bird and bat use. Further surveys to assess bird and bat mortality after a turbine is put into operation are also recommended (California Energy Commission and the California Department of Fish and Game 2007).

McEvoy Ranch, a 550 acre ranch located in northeastern Marin County, California approximately 5 miles southwest of Petaluma, operates a single Norwin 29-Stall-225kW wind turbine, which has a rotor diameter of 29m and a maximum rotor tip height of 45m.  Prior to the construction of the McEvoy Ranch turbine, Point Blue (then called PRBO Conservation Science) conducted a study during the winter, spring, and fall of 2006 to assess diurnal bird use at the turbine’s proposed site.  The 2006 study found that up to 28 species of birds used the airspace around the proposed windmill site, including 12 species of raptors, 4 of which are special status species- Golden Eagle, Peregrine Falcon, White-tailed Kite, and Northern Harrier (Cormier 2007, Shuford and Gardali 2008).  Raptor concentrations at the site, however, were not particularly high in comparison to other sites in Marin County, and thus it did not appear that the proposed

wind turbine would pose a significant threat to local raptor populations (GGRO 2005, Cormier 2007).  Nonetheless, the pre-construction study concluded that there would still be the potential for avian mortality resulting from the turbine and therefore avian mortality should be carefully evaluated once the turbine was built and put into operation (Cormier et al. 2007).  Furthermore, the county supervisors upon approving the permit required a post-construction bird and bat mortality monitoring program. Marin County now requires the submittal of a bird and bat study prior to permit approvals for all wind energy conversion systems (WECS) within the county (Title 22.32.180).

The McEvoy Ranch wind turbine was completed and commissioned in June of 2009. Systematic carcass searches and observer efficiency tests were conducted from early July of 2009 through October 2012, and the results are summarized in this report.

## Methods

On-the-ground carcass searches around wind turbines are used to document and assess the presence of deceased birds and bats resulting from collisions with turbines.  The methods used for carcass searches at McEvoy Ranch followed  standardized monitoring techniques recommended by the California Energy Commission and the California Department of Fish and Game (2007), along with similar methods used in other recent windmill-related bird fatality studies (Smallwood and Thelander 2008).

Site Description: A flat, sparsely vegetated area encircles the base of the turbine and extends asymmetrically 15-50 m out away from the turbine (Figure 1).  This flat area was devoid of vegetation for approximately the first 6 months of surveys, after which the area began filling in with relatively sparse grass cover.  Beyond the flat area, the terrain slopes downward on 3 sides of the search area and is vegetated primarily with a mix of grass species approximately 2 feet tall.  Light seasonal cattle grazing was applied to the

area surrounding the turbine beginning in 2011, which reduced overall grass height and density in the search area.

Carcass Search Plot: For the first year of surveys, carcass searches took place within a circular 50 m radius search plot centered at the wind turbine.  A 50 m radius was originally chosen because previous studies at other wind farms found 85%-96% of carcasses ≤50 m from the turbine base (Orloff and Flannery 1992, Smallwood and Thelander 2004).  The California Energy Commission and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (2007) recommend that search plots have a radius at least half as large as the maximum rotor tip height.  Under this guideline, a 50 m search radius with a 45 m maxium rotor tip height provided more than adequate coverage. After evaluating results from the first year of surveys (July 2009 – July 2010) in which all carcasses were found within 15 m of the turbine base (details given in the Results section below), the search radius was reduced to a 30 m search radius.  This smaller search radius was still in compliance with the state guidelines outlined above and allowed observers to focus more effort within a smaller area and thus improve search efficiency.

Conducting Searches: Carcass searches were primarily conducted by McEvoy Ranch personnel.  Each observer received one day of field training by a Point Blue biologist prior to conducting carcass searches on their own.  In order to facilitate a systematic search of the entire plot area, color coded survey flags were used to demarcate the search plot along 5 concentric circles spaced away from the turbine at distances of 10m, 20 m, 30 m, 40 m, and 50 m (Figure 1).  Observers scanned for carcasses on the ground while slowly walking around the turbine between the concentric circular transects outlined by the survey flags, such that the observer  would encircle the turbine along a path at an approximate distance of 5 m, 15 m, 25 m, 35 m, and 45 m.  Observers were instructed to meander slightly while walking each concentric circle in order to maximize the area searched.  In addition to the colored survey flags, a GPS unit was used to help guide the searcher within the carcass search plot.  A survey log was

maintained to record the observer’s name, date, start and stop time, total minutes surveyed, weather conditions, and other field notes.

Frequency of Carcass Searches:  Through the first year of monitoring, Point Blue recommended that surveys should be conducted five days per week during peak migration season (April and May for spring and September and October for fall), and at least once a week during the non-peak migration season.  Due to the limited number of carcasses found after the initial year of surveys, Point Blue recommended reducing survey effort to three days per week during peak migration and once every two weeks for the rest of the year when typically less bird movement occurs.  Overall survey frequency, however, varied somewhat and deviated from the recommended frequency depending on weather, personnel availability, and other logistical constraints.  Also, surveys were halted whenever the turbine was offline; i.e. not in operation (Table 1).

Collecting Carcass Data:  Any carcass found was collected, placed in a sealed plastic bag with a unique specimen tag and identification number, stored in a freezer, digitally photographed, and transferred to Point Blue Conservation Science for holding.  At the time of collection, the following data were recorded:  date, time, observer, species, sex, age, description of injury(ies), and distance from turbine tower.  A numeric code for carcass condition and detectability was assigned to each carcass as proposed by Anderson et al. (1999).

Bias Correction:  In order to correct for searcher efficiency biases, we conducted random on-site trials to test observers by volitionally planting bird carcasses randomly within the search plot.  These tests were done without the searchers prior knowledge. Three size classes of bird carcasses were used for the trials; small (e.g. warbler, sparrow, finch), medium (e.g. pigeon, scrub-jay), and large birds (e.g. crows, gulls, pheasant).  Due to concerns over potentially conditioning scavengers to search for carcasses near the turbine, we limited the searcher efficiency trials to 3 per searcher per year.  For this

same reason, we did not perform extensive scavenger removal trials; artificially supplying a food source for scavengers may have conditioned scavengers to systematically look for carcasses around the turbine and thereby inherently bias our carcass surveys.  However, we evaluated the presence/absence of scavenger activity during the searcher efficiency trials by revisiting carcasses volitionally planted for the searcher efficiency trials; such carcasses were checked daily for one up to one week and then removed.

## Results

Search Effort: Between 7 July 2009 and 1 October 2012 (39 months), a total of 187 carcass search surveys were conducted (Table 1).  The average (mean) time spent searching for carcasses during each survey was 35 minutes (standard error = 0.96), with a cumulative search time during the 39 month period of 108 hours and 42 minutes. Four different observers conducted the surveys, where the primary observer (Jeff Creque PhD , McEvoy Ranch) conducted 81% of the surveys, a secondary observer (Ryan DiGaudio M.S., Point Blue biologist) conducted 15% of the surveys, and the remaining 4% of surveys were conducted by other McEvoy personnel (Mark Rohrmeier and Shari DeJoseph).

Carcass Detections:  Over the 39 month period of carcass searches around the turbine, no bird carcasses were found.  However three bat carcasses were found; one was a Mexican free-tailed bat (Tadarida brasiliensis), and two individuals were Western red bats (Lasiurus blossevilli), a California species of special concern (CDFW 2011).  Two of the bats (a red bat and the Mexican free-tailed bat) were found on the same day, 19 September 2009.  These individuals were discovered on the flat pad near the base of the turbine at a distance of 2.5m and 15m away from the base.   Their carcasses were found in excellent condition and were both fresh and intact.  Another Western red bat was found on 8 September, 2010.  This individual was found ~7 m south of the turbine base and had been partially scavenged by rodents or insects around its head.  It was also missing its right wing, though it is difficult to say if this was a result of scavenging or

from a collision injury.  The three bat carcasses are temporarily being stored in Point Blue’s specimen freezer at the Palomarin field station until they are transferred to the collections of California Academy of Sciences.

Observer efficiency: Each McEvoy Ranch personnel conducting carcass searchers underwent searcher efficiency trials, where the trials were conducted unannounced to observers.  Trials took place in late summer/early fall when grass was brown and dry, and also in the spring when grass was green and relatively denser than during the fall surveys.  Observer efficiency, defined as the percentage of volitionally planted carcasses that searchers found, averaged 70% (standard error = 11.5) across all bird sizes. According to relative bird size, 100% of large bird carcasses were found, 70% of medium bird carcasses were found, and 42% of small bird carcasses were found.

Carcass removal by scavengers:  We were cautious against conditioning scavengers to search for carcasses near the turbine and therefore did not conduct standardized carcass removal tests, as this would have required us to regularly plant large numbers of carcasses near the turbine.  However, we documented scavenger removal of carcasses that were volitionally planted for searcher efficiency trials.  In a 2 day searcher efficiency trial in August 2009, 3 out of 5 planted carcasses were removed by scavengers within 2 days.  In September 2009, 2 out of 12 carcasses were removed by scavengers within a 7 day trial period.  In April 2010, zero carcasses out of 10 were removed over a 5 day trial period.  In April 2012, zero carcasses out of 5 were removed over a 5 day period.  Of the 5 bird carcasses removed over the course of searcher efficiency trials, 4 were small birds and 1 was a medium sized bird; no large bird carcasses were removed by scavengers. This anecdotal evidence suggests that scavengers preferentially removed small birds over the large and medium sized birds, though more study is needed to quantify the true bias imposed by scavenger removal.

## Discussion

During the first 39 months of the McEvoy wind turbine operation, the observed avian mortality rate was zero- a strong indication that this particular wind turbine is not

having an adverse effect on local bird populations.  Variance in bird and bat fatalities between wind energy projects may be attributed to a variety of factors, such as food availability and site topography, and where raptors occur fatalities may be attributed to factors such as specific flight behavior of individuals (Hoover and Morrison 2005).  It seems that wind farms consisting of an array of multiple wind turbines positioned in tightly spaced rows along ridge lines (e.g. the Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area) pose much more of an obstacle and potential threat to flying birds than do isolated individual wind turbines, such as the McEvoy Ranch wind turbine.  Furthermore, the 225kW McEvoy turbine is smaller in both height and rotor sweep volume than the 1.5MW turbines commonly examined in other morality studies, and thus may pose less risk to flying birds and bats (Millikin personal com.). And though few studies exist on the average height of night-migrating birds in the West, a recent study in the Great Lakes region found the average height of night-migrating birds to be 145 m, 100 m higher than the McEvoy turbine’s maximum rotor height (Millikin and Gehring, in prep).

Despite the null finding of avian mortality events at the McEvoy wind turbine, it is possible that a small number of bird carcasses could have been undetected and/or were removed by scavengers between surveys.  This is particularly true for small birds because searcher efficiency was only 41% for small birds, and it appears that scavengers may preferentially remove small birds over larger birds based on scavenger removals that occurred during the searcher efficiency trials.   However, these apparent biases alone cannot be used to estimate avian mortality rates given that no avian mortality events were ever documented.

Three bat carcasses were discovered over the 39 month monitoring period- two were found in September 2009 and one in September 2010.  The fact that two of the three bats were found on the same day (September 19[th] , 2009) suggests there may have been a unique set of circumstances (e.g. weather conditions, prey insect concentrations, and/or time of year) that led to their fatality.  The species found (Mexican free-tailed

and Western red bats) are both migratory, and thus would have been on their southward migration in September.  It is possible that these two individuals were part of a larger group of bats migrating or foraging together, perhaps tracking a concentration of aerial insects.  Radar-acoustic studies indicate that bats fly lower than night-migrating birds and thus are at a relatively higher risk to wind turbine mortality (Millikin 2012). High winds and low-ceiling overcast conditions can cause bats to fly at lower altitudes, thus exposing them to even greater risk of collisions with wind turbines (Millikin 2012). Though we did not collect nocturnal weather data as part of this study, conditions at the turbine on the morning of September 19[th] were described as foggy and overcast with light winds (10-15mph).  Inclement weather has been associated with bird strikes on human-made structures, including windmills, and a similar relationship likely exists for bats (Erickson et al. 2001, Millikin 2012).   The preliminary site assessment for the McEvoy wind turbine prior to its construction concluded that there was a relatively low risk of diurnal birds colliding with the turbine (Cormier et al. 2007). However, nocturnal bird and bat use at the site was unknown, thus the observed bat mortality events were unforeseen.  Therefore, we suggest that preliminary site assessments for future proposed wind turbines in areas that might concentrate birds or bats during migration employ specialized acoustic radar equipment designed for detecting nocturnal birds and bats (Millikin 2003).

## Conclusions

After a 39 month period of intensive mortality monitoring at the McEvoy wind turbine, we found no evidence for any diurnal bird mortality and extremely low mortality rates for bats, with just 3 individual bats found in over three years.  Though there is a small probability that some mortality events were undetected, the overall impact this single wind turbine has had on birds and bats during the study period appears to have been extremely small (in the case of bats) to possibly nil for birds. Though formal carcass surveys have been discontinued, we recommend that incidental discoveries of bird or bat carcasses (should they occur) be documented and reported.

In considering the broader scope of wildlife impacts caused by wind turbines at large, it is prudent to also consider the broad scale externalized environmental impacts caused by conventional non-renewable energy sources (i.e. fossil and nuclear energy), which includes habitat destruction, air and water pollution, and climate change- all of which have significant negative impacts on bird populations (see Sovacool 2009 and 2012 for review).  Wind energy development can be an appropriate alternative energy source if conducted in such a manner that impacts to wildlife are minimized.  Marin County strives to achieve this goal through its ordinance (22.32.180) drafted to govern responsible development of single turbine wind energy conversion systems (WECS) within the county. In following the guidelines set forth by this ordinance, the McEvoy wind turbine may serve as a model for future similar WECS projects.

## Future Siting Recommendations

Guidelines set forth by the California Energy Commission and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (2007) recommend against siting turbines in areas that might concentrate bird or bat activity, such as on a ridgeline or near roosting or nesting sites. To help ensure these recommendations are followed, the Marin County WECS development ordinance (22.32.180) issued the following general standards, stating that no “small, medium, or large WECS or supporting infrastructure shall be allowed:

a. Within five times the total height or 300 feet, whichever is greater, of a known nest or roost of a listed State or Federal threatened or endangered species or California Department of Fish and Game designated bird or bat ‘species of special concern’ (unless siting of the WECS preceded nest or roost establishment) based on the findings and conclusions of the required Bird and Bat Study as defined in Section 22.32.180 G.9.

b. Within five times the total height or 300 feet, whichever is greater, of a known or suspected avian migratory concentration point  based on the findings and conclusions of the required Bird and Bat Study as defined in Section 22.32.180 G.9.

c. Within 1.5 times the total height or 100 feet, whichever is greater, of a Stream Conservation Area (SCA), a Wetlands Conservation Area (WCA), a State or Federal listed special status species habitat area, a designated archaeological or historical site, or a water course, wetland, pond, lake, bay front area habitat island, or other significant water body with suitable avian habitat based on the findings and conclusions of Bird and Bat Study as defined in Section 22.32.180 G.9. “

Furthermore, the county ordinance prohibits any turbine >40 ft high from being placed less than 300 ft horizontally or 100 ft vertically away from ridgelines. These standards were piloted in siting the McEvoy Ranch turbine, and thus helped minimize its impact to birds and bats.
